sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The Hearth is one of the two practical-arts tracks (§6): the competencies of running a home: feeding people, clothing them, keeping the place in order, and receiving guests well. Its through-line, in the outline's words, is that a woman should be the one who knows how to make a house work.

In Grade 3 the child moves from helping to doing: a paring knife and the stovetop under direct supervision, and hand-sewing (§6, grade phasing for Grades 2–3). Grade 3 also adds two new courses to the track: Food Preservation (freezing and drying) and Care of Children and the Sick (§5, Grade 3).

Enrollment. The outline presents the Hearth to girls and the Workshop to boys by default, and any family may choose either track, or both, without friction or explanation (§6). As the outline notes, competence at the hearth and in the yard were never mutually exclusive.

blocks.text: The outline's grade phasing is the rule (§6):
The paring knife and the stovetop, always with an adult beside the child. The oven is the adult's job; the child watches and helps with oven mitts.

Knife rules: a cutting board on a damp towel so it won't slide; the "claw" grip, with fingertips tucked; cut away from the body; never catch a falling knife; wash knives separately, never in a sink full of water.
Food safety: wash hands first; keep raw meat and eggs away from other food; wipe up spills at once.
Heat: pot handles turned inward; oven mitts, not towels; steam lifts away from the face.
Needles and pins go back in the pincushion; scissors are passed handle first.
Care of the sick: the child helps, the parent cares. The child learns basic first aid and when to fetch an adult or call for help, not to treat anything serious.
Practical arts aren't graded.
Skills checklist each term: can the child do the term's skills safely and confidently?
The Hearth book: each recipe made, written out by hand with a sentence about how it went, and each sewing piece, photographed or sketched. It goes in the portfolio.
The Term 6 meal is the year's culminating work for Grade 3, a first step toward the Grade 5 culminating meal: planned, shopped for, cooked and served (§6).

reference.title: Kitchen rules (teach in week 1, post on the wall)

blocks.text: 1. An adult is in the kitchen whenever the stove or a knife is in use.
2. Wash hands before cooking, and after touching raw meat or eggs.
3. Apron on, sleeves up, long hair tied back.
4. Pot handles turned in; oven mitts, not towels.
5. A cutting board on a damp towel so it can't slide.
6. Clean as you go; wipe spills at once.

reference.title: Table and hospitality: setting the table

blocks.text: Each week the child sets the family table: fork on the left; knife (blade facing the plate) and spoon on the right; cup above the knife; napkin beside the fork or on the plate. By week 6 the child does it without a reminder.
Kitchen rules. Go through the six rules. Show where things live: knives, pots, measuring cups, oven mitts. Wash hands properly (soap, twenty seconds, between the fingers).
Wash and dry the dishes after a family meal: hottest water the hands can bear, glasses first, then plates, then pots. Set the table for dinner.

The paring knife. Hold the handle firmly; the other hand in a "claw", fingertips tucked under, guiding the food. For round foods, cut a flat side first so they don't roll. Start on soft foods: banana, cucumber, strawberries. Never catch a falling knife.
Cut fruit for a family fruit salad.

Reading a recipe and measuring. Read the whole recipe aloud first, and gather everything. Dry ingredients: scoop, then level off with a knife. Liquids: a clear cup on the counter, read at eye level. (Arithmetic's cups and pints come in Term 4.)
Applesauce (recipe below). The child peels with a peeler and chops; the adult stays beside the stove.
The stovetop. Handles turned in; start on low or medium heat; stir with a long wooden spoon; lift a lid away from the face to let the steam out. The adult turns the burner on and off.
Vegetable soup (recipe below).
Harvesting herbs: in the morning, after the dew dries, snip stems just above a pair of leaves so the plant keeps growing. Rinse gently and pat dry. (From a garden, a pot, or a bunch bought fresh.)
Hang herbs to dry: tie small bunches with string and hang them upside down in a warm, dry, airy place. They'll be ready in two or three weeks, for Term 2.
Skills checklist (below).
Make applesauce or soup for the family, set the table, and serve. Write both recipes in the Hearth book in the child's own hand, with a sentence about how it went.
Applesauce (serves 4)
6 apples, peeled, cored and chopped · ½ cup water · 1 teaspoon cinnamon · 1–2 tablespoons sugar or honey (optional).
Put everything in a pot over medium-low heat. Cover and simmer, stirring now and then, about 20 minutes, until the apples are soft. Mash with a potato masher. Serve warm or cold.
Vegetable soup (serves 4)
1 onion, 2 carrots, 2 celery sticks, 2 potatoes, all chopped · 1 tablespoon oil · 4 cups broth · salt and pepper · a handful of fresh herbs.

In a large pot over medium heat, cook the onion in the oil until soft (about 5 minutes). Add the other vegetables and the broth. Bring to a gentle boil, then lower the heat and simmer about 25 minutes, until the potatoes are soft. Add salt, pepper and herbs to taste.

terms.title: Late Autumn · Food Preservation: Freezing and Drying, and Biscuits

head: Strands

Freezing fruit · blanching and freezing vegetables · drying apple rings · storing dried herbs · mixing and baking biscuits
Real work
A tray of frozen berries · frozen vegetables · dried apple rings · jars of dried herbs · biscuits for a family meal
Table and hospitality

glance.text: Science link. Science Term 2 shows that water freezes and expands; Term 3 shows evaporation. Freezing slows spoiling by cold; drying stops it by taking the water away.
Oven and boiling water are the adult's jobs. The child prepares, watches and helps with oven mitts.

reference.title: Table and hospitality: serving and clearing

blocks.text: Serve a plate from the guest's left; clear from the right. Carry one or two plates at a time, never stacked high. Clear the serving dishes first, then the plates, then the cups. Practice at every family dinner this term.
Why freezing works: cold slows the tiny living things that spoil food. Flash freezing: spread berries on a tray so they don't stick together, freeze for two hours, then pour into a bag.
Freeze a tray of berries or sliced fruit. Label the bag with what it is and the date.
Blanching vegetables: a quick dip in boiling water (adult), then straight into ice water to stop the cooking. It keeps the color and taste when frozen.
Blanch and freeze green beans or carrots. The child trims and cuts; the adult handles the boiling water; the child does the ice bath, drains and bags. Label and date.

Drying: taking the water out of food so it keeps for months. Apples are sliced thin and dipped in lemon water so they don't turn brown. (Science Term 4 tests this with a cut apple: the half with lemon juice stays pale.)
Dry apple rings (method below).
Storing dried herbs: when the Term 1 bunches are crisp, strip the leaves, crumble them, and store in clean, dry jars away from light.
Fill and label herb jars with the name and the date.
Biscuits: cutting cold butter into flour with a fork or a pastry cutter until it looks like crumbs; stirring in milk just until it comes together; patting the dough out (not rolling hard).
Bake biscuits (recipe below). The adult handles the oven.
Skills checklist (below).
A family meal with biscuits, the Term 1 applesauce or soup, and dried apple rings for dessert. The child sets the table, serves and clears. Write the term's recipes in the Hearth book.
Dried apple rings
4 apples · 4 cups water with the juice of 1 lemon.

Core the apples (an apple corer, or the adult with a knife) and slice into rings about ⅛ inch thick. Dip in the lemon water and pat dry. Lay on a wire rack on a baking sheet. Dry in the oven at its lowest setting (about 170–200 °F) for 2–3 hours, turning once, until leathery. Cool completely before storing in a jar.
Biscuits (about 10)
2 cups flour · 1 tablespoon baking powder · ½ teaspoon salt · 6 tablespoons cold butter · ¾ cup milk.

Heat the oven to 425 °F (adult). Mix the dry ingredients. Cut in the butter until crumbly. Stir in the milk just until the dough comes together. Pat out on a floured board about ¾ inch thick, cut rounds with a glass, and place on a baking sheet. Bake 12–15 minutes, until golden (adult).

glance.text: Fine Arts link. The cross-stitch sampler in Fine Arts Term 2 was the child's first needlework. This term builds the plain stitches every household needs.

blocks.text: Needles and pins always go back in the pincushion, never in the mouth or on the table.
Pass scissors handle first, closed.
Use a thimble on the middle finger to push the needle.
Count needles out and back in.

reference.title: Table and hospitality: welcoming a guest

blocks.text: Open the door with a smile and a greeting. Offer to take the guest's coat and hang it up. Show them where to sit, and offer something to drink. Practice with family members playing guests.

The sewing kit, threading and knotting. Cut thread about as long as your arm. Lick or snip the end straight, push it through the eye (a needle threader helps). Tie a knot at the long end: wrap it around a finger, roll it off, and pull tight.
Running stitch on a felt scrap: in and out along a pencil line, stitches the same length, about ¼ inch.
The backstitch: a strong stitch that makes a solid line. Bring the needle up, take a stitch back, come up a stitch ahead, and go back into the end of the last stitch.
Start a felt bookmark: cut a strip of felt and backstitch your initials and a simple border on it.

Sewing on a button. Mark the spot. Come up through the fabric and one hole, go down through the next; repeat six times. For a four-hole button, make an X or two lines. Finish with a few tight stitches on the back and a knot.
Sew a button on a real garment (a loose or missing one), or on a fabric scrap to practice first.

Mending a small tear. Turn the garment inside out. Pin the edges of the tear together. Sew over it with small, close running stitches or a whipstitch (over and over the edge), starting and ending a little beyond the tear.
Mend a real garment: a split seam or a small tear in play clothes.

Minding a younger child. Stay where you can see them at all times. Keep small objects out of reach; doors and stairs closed. Good things to do together: read aloud, build blocks, sing songs, play a simple game, go outside with a grown-up. Know where a parent is, and fetch them for anything worrying.
Mind a younger sibling (or a neighbor's child) for an hour, with a parent nearby in the house. Plan two activities beforehand.
Skills checklist (below).
Finish the felt bookmark and give it to someone. Add the term's sewing to the Hearth book (a sketch or a photo, and how it was made).

blocks.text: Mending is a real gift to a household. Keep a small mending basket where the child can find the next job.
Minding is about care, not control. A child who reads to a sibling and fetches a parent at the right time is doing it well.
Families with a baby can add holding and feeding an infant, with a parent beside them (§6).

terms.title: Late Winter · Laundry, Cleaning and Bread

head: Strands

rows: Skills
Sorting laundry and reading care labels · folding · treating a stain · a cleaning routine · kneading · shaping and baking bread
Real work
A family load sorted, folded and put away · a room kept clean on a routine · a loaf of bread from scratch
Table and hospitality

Tasks

glance.text: Science link. Science Term 4 is about chemical changes. Bread is one: yeast feeds on sugar and makes bubbles of gas that raise the dough.
The washing machine, dryer, iron and oven are run by the adult, with the child helping and watching.

reference.title: Table and hospitality: conversation with adults

blocks.text: At the table, ask an adult a real question ("What was your favorite book when you were my age?"), then listen to the answer and ask one more question about it. Don't interrupt; let others finish. Practice at family dinners, then with a guest.

Sorting laundry: whites, colors and darks; towels separate; delicates aside. Care labels: a tub means washing (dots show how warm), a triangle is bleach, a square with a circle is the dryer, an iron is ironing; an X over any of them means "don't".
Sort a family load, check pockets, and help load the machine. The adult sets and starts it.
Folding: shake out each piece first. Towels in thirds, then in half. T-shirts: face down, fold each side to the middle, then in half. Socks: match, then roll or fold together.
Fold a load and put it away, each person's clothes in their own pile.

Treating a stain: act quickly; blot, don't rub. Cold water for blood and most food; a drop of dish soap rubbed in for grease. Check the stain is gone before the garment goes in the dryer, because heat sets it. (Science Term 5 shows how soap lifts grease.)
Treat a real stain (or make a test one on a rag with a drop of oil or juice).
A cleaning routine for one room: tidy first (everything in its place), then clean from top to bottom (dust high places first, floor last), dry before wet (dust and sweep, then wipe and mop).
Clean one room on the routine, such as the child's bedroom or a bathroom sink and mirror, and make a weekly checklist for it. Keep it up through the term.

Yeast and kneading. Yeast is a tiny living thing: in warm water with a little sugar it foams. Kneading: push the dough away with the heels of the hands, fold it back, turn it a quarter turn, and repeat, for about 8–10 minutes, until it's smooth and springy.
Mix and knead the bread dough (recipe below), and set it to rise. Look at it after an hour: it should be twice the size.

Shaping and baking: press out the air, shape into a loaf, place in a greased pan, let it rise again, then bake (adult handles the oven). It's done when it sounds hollow when tapped underneath. Then the skills checklist (below).
Bake and serve the bread at a family meal. Write the recipe in the Hearth book.
A simple white loaf
1¼ cups warm water (comfortably warm, not hot) · 2¼ teaspoons (1 packet) dry yeast · 1 tablespoon sugar · 3 to 3¼ cups flour · 1½ teaspoons salt · 2 tablespoons oil or melted butter.

Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm water; wait 5–10 minutes until it foams. Add the oil, salt and 3 cups of flour, and mix into a dough, adding a little more flour if it's very sticky. Knead 8–10 minutes. Put in an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise in a warm place about 1 hour, until doubled. Press out the air, shape into a loaf, and put in a greased loaf pan. Cover and let rise about 30 minutes. Bake at 375 °F for 30–35 minutes (adult). Cool on a rack before slicing.

Real work

glance.text: Workshop link. The Workshop track digs a kitchen-garden bed in its weeks 29–30. The Hearth starts its herbs indoors in pots in week 25 and moves them into that bed in week 30.
The child helps; the parent cares. In Care of the Sick, the child learns to bring comfort and to fetch an adult, not to treat anything serious.

reference.title: Table and hospitality: flowers on the table

blocks.text: Pick or buy a few flowers or green branches in season. Trim the stems at a slant, strip leaves that would sit in the water, and arrange them low enough that people can see each other across the table. Change the water every two days.
Planning a herb pot. Good first herbs: basil, parsley, chives, and mint (in a pot of its own, because it spreads). Most herbs want sun (a south or west window) and soil that drains.
Plant herbs in pots from seeds or small seedlings: soil to an inch below the rim, seeds pressed in lightly or seedlings set at the same depth they were growing, watered gently. Label each pot.
Watering and care: water when the top of the soil feels dry, at the base, not on the leaves; turn the pot so plants grow straight; once seedlings have a few leaves, snip extras so each has room.
Keep a watering chart on the windowsill for the rest of the term.
Simple nursing: a quiet room, curtains drawn a little; a cool damp cloth for a hot forehead; water within reach; soft voices. Wash hands after helping, so the illness doesn't spread.
Make a "sick tray" kit to keep ready: a small tray, a cup with a lid or straw, a napkin, a little bell, a book or a puzzle, and a card the child has made.

Basic first aid: for a scrape, wash with clean water and cover with a bandage; for a nosebleed, sit up, lean slightly forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for ten minutes. When to fetch an adult: anything bleeding a lot, a bad fall, a burn, trouble breathing, or anyone who can't wake up. The child learns the family's address and phone number, and how to call the emergency number.
Practice cleaning and bandaging a "scrape" on a doll or a sibling's arm, and say the emergency steps aloud. Make a checklist for the family first-aid kit and check it's all there.
Cooking for someone who's unwell: plain, gentle food: toast, broth, applesauce from Term 1, weak tea with honey. Small portions, brought on the tray.
Prepare a tray meal for a family member: for someone actually unwell, or as a practice treat for a parent.

Transplanting: water the pot first; tip the plant out gently holding the base of the stems; set it in a hole in the bed at the same depth; firm the soil; water well. Then the skills checklist (below).
Move the herb seedlings into the Workshop's garden bed (keep one pot on the windowsill). Add the term to the Hearth book.

blocks.text: The sick tray is charity made practical. Keep it ready; children are proud when it's needed.
Emergency knowledge matters most. A child who knows the address, the phone number and when to get help has learned the most important first aid there is.

Pots with drainage holes and saucers · potting soil · herb seeds or seedlings · labels · a small watering can · a tray, a lidded cup or straw, a napkin, a bell · a family first-aid kit (bandages, clean cloths, gloves) · a vase · ingredients for toast, broth or tea

terms.title: Summer · A Meal for Guests, a Sewing Project and Thank-You Notes

head: Strands
Table and Hospitality (§6) · Cooking (§6) · Sewing and Needlework (§6)
rows: Skills
Planning a menu and a shopping list · shopping to a budget · sewing a simple bag · cooking ahead · hosting guests · writing thank-you notes
Real work
A hand-sewn drawstring bag · a simple meal served to guests: soup, biscuits and a dried-fruit dessert · thank-you notes sent
Table and hospitality
Thank-you notes, by hand (and setting the table each week)
Tasks
A skill · B real work (2 a week × 6 = 12)

glance.text: Toward Grade 5. The outline's culminating Hearth work in Grade 5 is to plan, shop for, cook and serve a full meal to the family (§6). This term's guest meal is a first step, with the parent beside the child.

blocks.text: A good note is short and specific: "Dear Mrs. ___, Thank you for coming to lunch. I liked hearing about your garden. Love, ___." Written by hand, addressed and sent within a week. (Penmanship Term 5 taught the friendly-letter form.)

Planning the meal. Choose a menu from dishes the child has made this year: vegetable soup (Term 1), biscuits (Term 2), and dried apple rings or applesauce for dessert. Decide on guests (grandparents, a neighbor, friends) and a date in week 35. Write the shopping list.
Shop with a parent to a budget the parent sets: check prices, compare two brands, and add up the total. (Arithmetic: money and making change, Term 2.)

The drawstring bag: cut a rectangle of cotton about 10 by 20 inches. Fold over and stitch a channel (a "casing") along each short end. Fold the fabric in half, right sides together, and backstitch the two sides up to the casings.
Cut and start the bag.
Finishing the bag: turn it right side out, push the corners out, and thread a cord through the casing with a safety pin on its end. Tie the ends.
Finish the bag. It can hold the child's sewing kit, or be a gift.
Cooking ahead: some dishes can be made a day early. Soup tastes better the next day; biscuit dough can be cut and kept in the refrigerator until baking.
Practice run: make the soup for the family, and note anything to do differently for the guests.

Hosting, putting the year together: set the table properly (Term 1), with flowers (Term 5); welcome the guests and take their coats (Term 3); serve from the left and clear from the right (Term 2); make conversation with the adults (Term 4).
Cook and serve the meal to the guests, with the parent helping at the stove and the oven.

weeks.title: Thank-you notes and the year's review

blocks.text: The year's skills checklist (below).
Write thank-you notes to the guests, and to someone who helped with the Hearth this year. Finish the Hearth book with the meal's menu and a sentence about how it went.

blocks.text: Let the child be the host. Stay in the kitchen as much as possible on the day; the guests are coming to see what the child can do.
Small and successful beats grand. Soup, biscuits and apples, served warmly, is a fine first meal for guests.
Keep the Hearth book. Over Grades 3–5 it becomes the child's own cookbook.
Cotton fabric (about 10 × 20 inches), thread, pins, scissors, a cord and a safety pin · ingredients for soup, biscuits and dessert · flowers · note cards, envelopes and stamps · the Hearth book
